Right: the same two trees plus an edge between D and E, which closes the triangle B, D, E (shown in the accent color), so is_forest() returns False." width="100%"} A forest is an acyclic, undirected graph (disjoint union of trees). For a graph with *n* nodes and *k* connected components to be a forest it: - must be undirected - must have exactly *n - k* edges - must be acyclic The method counts the connected components and compares the edge count with *n - k*; any surplus edge necessarily closes a cycle. Unlike `is_tree()`, a forest may consist of several separate pieces, and isolated nodes count as one-node trees. Typical uses: - checking that a graph has no cycles at all, regardless of how many components it has - validating collections of hierarchies (e.g. several family trees or taxonomies) - confirming that an edge-removal or spanning-forest step left no redundant links Self-loops and parallel edges are cycles, so they make the result `False`. Directed graphs always return `False` (except the empty graph); for directed acyclicity use `is_dag()`. The whole graph is checked and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if graph is a forest, `False` otherwise. An empty graph is a forest. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A forest is exactly the disjoint union of trees, so a single tree is a forest with $k = 1$, and the empty graph is a forest with $k = 0$. The edge-count law $|E| = n - k$ drops straight out of applying $|E| = n_i - 1$ to each of the $k$ component trees and summing over $i$; combined with acyclicity this is what the check actually verifies. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A single tree already satisfies the forest definition, since a tree is just a forest with one component: ::: {#1777cca7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) tree.is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Unlike `is_tree()`, this doesn't require a single connected component -- several disjoint trees together still form a forest: ::: {#8089ce34 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} forest = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), # first tree ("C", "D"), # second, disjoint tree ] ) ) forest.is_forest(), forest.is_tree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: A cycle breaks the "acyclic" requirement, so it's neither a forest nor a tree: ::: {#ee095d74 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) cycle.is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: An empty graph vacuously satisfies the definition too: ::: {#6a67cede .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph(directed=False).is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: A directed graph is never reported as a forest, even if its shape would qualify; use `is_dag()` to check a directed graph for cycles: ::: {#226acab7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_path_graph(n=3) directed.is_forest(), directed.is_dag() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (False, True) ``` ::: :::
